frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons and uses gas exports to preserve diplomatic leverage with Europe. Price volatility and dependence on hydrocarbon revenue remain constraints on long-term autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger pressures Algeria’s borders and complicates its non-intervention posture. Competing Russian, European, and regional security agendas increase the risk of strategic encirclement.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US and European interest as an alternative route for critical minerals from the Copperbelt. Angola gains infrastructure and bargaining power, but external financing and geopolitical competition may limit policy freedom.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Debt Legacy
frictionVectors.details: Debt repayment and infrastructure ties with Chinese lenders continue to shape Angola’s fiscal choices. Oil-sector diversification and contract reforms are improving sovereignty, but export dependence remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Export Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Benin-Niger oil export corridor has become entangled in diplomatic tensions and border restrictions. Its economic value is significant, but political disputes expose Benin’s infrastructure to regional coercion.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Militant Infiltration
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups operating from the Sahel are increasing pressure on northern Benin and its protected areas. Security dependence on foreign training, intelligence, and equipment is growing as domestic capacity is stretched.

frictionVectors.title: Debswana Partnership Balance
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with De Beers and secured greater domestic value from diamond production. However, market weakness and continued reliance on a major foreign partner leave revenue sovereignty exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Water scarcity and dependence on regional electricity imports can constrain mineral-processing ambitions. New solar, coal, and critical-mineral projects offer greater autonomy but also invite external capital and environmental scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control, local processing, and revenue capture from gold while restricting or reviewing foreign operators. Weak oversight and insecurity create space for illicit production and opaque patronage networks.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence and Territorial Loss
frictionVectors.details: Burkina Faso’s reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western influence but has not resolved militant control in parts of the country. Conflict disrupts mining, transport, and agricultural infrastructure while narrowing sovereign policy options.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi security rupture
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border support continue to restrict trade and regional cooperation. Burundi's security posture remains heavily shaped by tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals oversight gap
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral exports remain vulnerable to informal networks and smuggling. Limited state capacity and dependence on foreign buyers weaken sovereign control over resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic port competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde seeks to convert its location into logistics and maritime-security leverage while competing with larger West African ports. External investment brings infrastructure benefits but can create strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains reliant on imported fuel and vulnerable to shipping disruptions and price shocks. Renewable expansion is improving resilience but has not eliminated external energy dependence.

highlights: Oil and gas leverage under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and infrastructure risk
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten transport corridors, plantations, and public infrastructure. The conflict reduces effective state control and creates openings for armed groups and external commercial actors.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon exports and major infrastructure projects remain tied to foreign capital, neighboring transit routes, and external contractors. Cameroon captures revenue but retains limited bargaining power over financing, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain central to regime protection and counterinsurgency, strengthening Bangui's short-term position while increasing strategic dependence. The arrangement is widely associated with privileged access to gold and diamond networks.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group control of mining zones
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks retain influence over remote mineral areas and transport routes. Weak administration and limited infrastructure prevent the state from reliably formalizing production or collecting revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Post-transition legitimacy crisis
frictionVectors.details: The consolidation of power after the transitional period continues to generate domestic and regional scrutiny. Political centralization limits oversight of oil revenues and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad remains a key security partner for Western and regional actors while balancing ties with Gulf states and Russia-linked networks. Foreign military and financial relationships improve regime resilience but constrain independent strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: FRENCH ADMINISTRATION OF MAYOTTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to claim Mayotte, while France maintains administrative and security control. The dispute limits bilateral trust and complicates maritime governance.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies heavily on remittances, foreign aid, and imported energy. Gulf, French, and other external partners retain significant influence over infrastructure and fiscal choices.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing external powers

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CONFLICT AND RWANDAN PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: M23 activity and regional military tensions continue to weaken Kinshasa's effective control in North Kivu and South Kivu. Cross-border security competition directly threatens mining zones and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other strategic minerals draw intense Chinese, Western, and regional interest. The state is seeking greater value capture, but weak oversight and informal production continue to limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil companies and volatile export revenues remain central to the fiscal system. Limited diversification leaves national development exposed to external markets and contract asymmetries.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects expand connectivity but increase dependence on external finance and contractors. Debt and opaque project terms constrain policy flexibility.

highlights: Cocoa and offshore energy remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: International buyers and new traceability rules press Abidjan to address farmer incomes, deforestation, and supply-chain transparency. Export dependence still limits the state's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Protecting offshore oil, ports, and shipping lanes requires sustained cooperation with foreign naval and security partners. Regional instability in the Sahel also increases pressure on northern borders.

highlights: Port access remains the core sovereign asset
Base competition boosts revenues but narrows autonomy

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE AND PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The presence of US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military or security partners generates revenue and leverage, but also makes Djibouti vulnerable to great-power rivalry and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: ETHIOPIAN TRADE AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports remain indispensable to Ethiopia, creating strong bargaining power but also dependence on a single regional market. Debt-linked infrastructure obligations and external creditors constrain long-term policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large IMF, Gulf, and other creditor exposure constrains policy autonomy and channels strategic assets toward monetization. Debt service and currency pressures remain central sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Disruption around the Red Sea threatens Suez revenues, while the GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved. Egypt is balancing military signaling with reliance on regional partners.

frictionVectors.title: Declining oil and gas output
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and limited diversification weaken state revenue and increase dependence on foreign operators, technical expertise, and investment.

frictionVectors.title: LNG infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gas monetization depends on a narrow offshore and processing base exposed to international partners, market shifts, and export-logistics vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Assab and Massawa competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's ports sit amid rivalry involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, and Red Sea security actors. External interest creates bargaining leverage but also pressure over access and alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold projects rely heavily on foreign capital and operators, limiting domestic value capture despite strict state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade corridors, electricity, finance, and labor links to South Africa sharply limit Eswatini's room for autonomous economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and textile exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export industries depend on preferential market access and external investors, leaving jobs and foreign exchange vulnerable to trade-policy changes.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD tensions
frictionVectors.details: The GERD gives Ethiopia greater control over a strategic resource and electricity platform, but unresolved operating arrangements with Egypt and Sudan sustain diplomatic and security risks.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral financing remains important for transport, energy, and industrial projects. Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain Addis Ababa's negotiating autonomy.

highlights: Civilian transition consolidates after military rule

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is pressing for greater state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and other extractive projects. Tighter terms could improve sovereignty but risk friction with established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and mineral logistics remain reliant on foreign capital, operators, and infrastructure expertise. Disruptions or financing conditions could constrain Gabon's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and opaque licensing arrangements continue to challenge coastal enforcement and local fishing livelihoods. Limited patrol capacity leaves revenue capture and marine sovereignty vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRADE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia depends heavily on external financing and regional transit links around Banjul port and the Senegalese hinterland. This limits autonomy in infrastructure planning and trade negotiations.

highlights: Gold policy shifts toward domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: ILLEGAL GOLD MINING
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey damages water systems and exposes gaps in state control over gold production. Efforts to formalize mining and increase domestic refining face resistance from entrenched local and external networks.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are competing for Ghana's lithium, bauxite, manganese, and gold assets while Accra seeks processing and stronger fiscal terms. Debt and IMF-linked constraints may reduce the government's negotiating leverage.

highlights: Bauxite exports expand under military oversight

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MINING CONCESSION POWER
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed bauxite and iron-ore projects dominate export growth and infrastructure planning. Although the junta is demanding more local content and state participation, Guinea remains dependent on external capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: SIMANDOU CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou rail-port system will determine how much value Guinea captures from its largest resource project. Chinese, Singaporean, and other consortium interests create both financing options and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: CASHEW VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenue exposed to foreign buyers and price swings. Weak storage, transport, and credit infrastructure reinforce external control.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND NARCOTICS NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's fragile institutions and limited maritime surveillance create openings for illicit trafficking and foreign patronage networks. These pressures erode customs authority and complicate efforts to secure strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial Chinese and commercial lending constrain policy space. Nairobi is seeking greater control over strategic infrastructure while avoiding refinancing shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Resource-Corridor Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and associated transport corridors remain vulnerable to security threats, local opposition, and competing Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Phase II
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose Lesotho to disputes over pricing, construction delays, and environmental impacts.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Political Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and regional contractors are influential, while domestic political instability limits Lesotho's ability to negotiate infrastructure and resource agreements from a position of strength.

highlights: Iron Ore Revival, Limited State Capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and related logistics are dominated by foreign firms, including major European and Chinese-linked operators. Fiscal gains are significant but remain vulnerable to commodity cycles and weak domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign concessionaires and development financiers shape port modernization and mining corridors, raising recurring concerns over transparency, land access, and the distribution of infrastructure benefits.

highlights: Oil Sovereignty Split by Rival Authorities

frictionVectors.title: Oil Blockades and Institutional Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed factions continue to use production sites, export terminals, and budget access as leverage. The National Oil Corporation remains the key national institution but operates under persistent political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian Strategic Entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkey retains major security and economic influence in western Libya, while Russian-linked forces remain embedded in the east and south. Their presence complicates unified control of borders, energy assets, and military infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are led by foreign investors, leaving Madagascar exposed to price volatility, environmental disputes, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Energy, and Digital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and regional actors compete around ports, power, telecommunications, and logistics. Weak public finances reduce the government's leverage when negotiating long-term infrastructure concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and other minerals while trying to secure stronger local processing, fiscal terms and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and fertilizer dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages and reliance on imported fuel, fertilizer and food leave the country exposed to lenders, commodity prices and disruptions along regional transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has displaced Western influence but creates opaque costs, sovereignty concerns and accusations of abuses around counterinsurgency operations.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and mining disputes
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pushing for greater state control and renegotiation of mining revenues, increasing friction with foreign operators while insecurity limits oversight and production reliability.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen state revenues, but foreign operators, cross-border governance and future gas-price volatility constrain national control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and logistics concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, green-hydrogen ambitions and port infrastructure depend heavily on external finance and foreign firms, creating exposure to project delays and bargaining asymmetries.

frictionVectors.title: Diego Garcia settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has advanced diplomatically, but the future legal and operational terms of the UK-US military base remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External economic exposure
frictionVectors.details: The island's dependence on imported energy, tourism, finance and maritime connectivity leaves it vulnerable to external shocks and competition over Indian Ocean logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting diplomatic recognition and infrastructure investment into stronger control over Western Sahara, while the Polisario Front and legal challenges contest the legitimacy of resource projects.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic sectors
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, renewables, ports and critical-mineral supply chains are expanding through European, Gulf and Chinese investment, creating growth while requiring careful protection of domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led LNG Enclave
frictionVectors.details: International energy consortia retain decisive control over LNG finance, technology, and marketing. Maputo's long-term fiscal gains remain dependent on security and contract stability.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and External Forces
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity in Cabo Delgado continues to constrain state access and project timelines. Rwanda and other external security partners expand Maputo's capacity while increasing dependence on outside protection.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium, and emerging oil interests are drawing competing foreign investors. Namibia is using licensing and local-beneficiation policies to retain more value, but capital and technology remain externally concentrated.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen projects rely heavily on European and other foreign finance, equipment, and offtake agreements. Infrastructure gaps could limit national control over pricing and downstream industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's rupture with France and reduced Western security ties have increased reliance on alternative partners, including Russia-linked channels. This broadens Niger's diplomatic autonomy but may trade one dependency for another.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Pipeline Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control over uranium and hydrocarbon revenues while relations with foreign operators remain tense. Export infrastructure and sanctions exposure continue to constrain the state's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Multinational Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: International firms still shape deepwater production, technical access, and investment flows, while theft and pipeline vandalism reduce public capture of oil value. Regulatory reform has improved state leverage but has not ended structural dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Infrastructure Deficit
frictionVectors.details: Refining, electricity, and gas-processing bottlenecks force Nigeria to rely on foreign capital, imported equipment, and uneven energy partnerships. Domestic industrial capacity is improving but remains insufficient for full resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role as a mineral trading and processing hub faces persistent international scrutiny over supply chains linked to eastern DRC conflict networks. Export controls and traceability demands could constrain Kigali's commercial flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign aid, investment, and security relationships remain important to Rwanda's development and regional posture. These ties provide leverage and capacity while exposing Kigali to diplomatic pressure over its conduct in the Great Lakes.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe continues to seek offshore petroleum investment, but commercially viable discoveries and production remain unproven. The government faces pressure to preserve transparent licensing and avoid overreliance on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA MARITIME DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Limited naval capacity leaves the archipelago dependent on external partners for maritime surveillance, fisheries protection, and anti-trafficking operations. Security cooperation improves resilience but creates leverage for larger outside powers.

frictionVectors.title: CONTRACT AND REVENUE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production gives Dakar greater leverage over foreign operators, while debt constraints and revenue-management demands limit room for maneuver. Renegotiation and local-content policies risk friction with investors if implementation becomes abrupt.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND COASTAL INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access, including foreign-linked fleets, remains a major sovereignty concern for coastal communities. Port, rail, and energy projects bring investment but also expose Senegal to financing, procurement, and strategic-influence pressures.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles is attempting to capture more value from tuna and other marine resources through licensing, processing, and conservation measures. Its small administrative and enforcement capacity makes it vulnerable to pressure from distant-water fishing interests.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN SECURITY BALANCE
frictionVectors.details: Port calls, surveillance cooperation, and infrastructure links draw interest from India, China, the United States, and other partners. Victoria must balance maritime-security benefits against concerns about strategic dependence and the militarization of its territory.

frictionVectors.title: MINING REVENUE AND LOCAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain central to export earnings, but foreign capital and technical dependence constrain domestic control over value chains. Disputes over royalties, land, labor, and environmental impacts continue to test the government's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, energy, and mining-corridor projects depend heavily on external financiers and operators. These investments can improve connectivity while creating long-term exposure to creditor conditions and opaque concession arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL AND LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is promoting offshore petroleum exploration and production-sharing agreements as a route to fiscal independence, but weak regulatory capacity and contested federal-state authority complicate control of future revenues. Security risks and unclear commercial viability continue to deter some investors.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, BASES, AND EXTERNAL SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, China, and Western partners remain involved in ports, logistics, training, and maritime security. External support is essential against piracy and al-Shabaab, yet fragmented agreements can dilute federal authority and intensify competition among Somali political actors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty versus foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing and local value capture from platinum-group metals, manganese and other strategic minerals. Foreign investment remains essential, creating tension over ownership, beneficiation rules and regulatory certainty.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port congestion continue to weaken sovereign control over mineral exports. Private-sector partnerships and external financing are increasingly important to restore infrastructure capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving oil revenues vulnerable to sabotage, blockades and bargaining by external actors. The resulting fiscal shock limits Juba's autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of oil operations
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms remain central to production, services and infrastructure, while weak institutions constrain domestic oversight. Political fragmentation and elite competition further reduce effective national control over petroleum assets.

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks and external sponsorship
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed actors and attract competing regional and global intermediaries. The conflict has sharply reduced civilian control over mining zones and state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated transport corridors are strategically contested as outside powers seek military, commercial or diplomatic leverage. War damage and fragmented authority threaten control of export routes and humanitarian access.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for local processing and stronger state participation in graphite, nickel and rare-earth projects. Negotiations with foreign investors create friction over tax terms, ownership, environmental standards and export controls.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The government is expanding rail and port capacity while balancing Chinese, Gulf and Western commercial interests. Delays around major LNG development and port concessions expose the risks of dependence on external finance and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains a major regional transshipment and corridor hub, but its performance depends heavily on foreign shipping, terminal and finance partners. Competition among external operators limits full national control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains a core sovereign resource, yet production, processing and marketing face pressure from external buyers and investment interests. Weak downstream capacity constrains domestic value capture.

highlights: Energy and financing dependence constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation remain important sources of leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress limits Tunis's room to resist externally shaped economic conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate and Energy Decline
frictionVectors.details: Weak phosphate output and dependence on imported energy undermine resource sovereignty. Efforts to preserve state control have not yet produced reliable investment or infrastructure renewal.

highlights: Oil corridor advances under foreign-led financing

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Ownership
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline relies on foreign operators, lenders, and contractors, concentrating strategic control outside Uganda. Financing restrictions and environmental litigation continue to raise costs and political tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expected petroleum revenues could strengthen state capacity, but transport, refining, and power infrastructure remain dependent on external capital and technology. Revenue-management credibility is a persistent sovereignty risk.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Copper Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors are competing for influence over Zambia's copper and critical-minerals sector. Lusaka has greater leverage, but local processing and transparent ownership remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Export-Corridor Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and dependence on regional transport corridors constrain mining expansion and sovereign value capture. Grid investment and corridor diversification are progressing but remain vulnerable to external financing conditions.

highlights: Foreign capital still dominates strategic mining

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Mining and Lithium Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major position in lithium, platinum, and other strategic minerals, giving external investors substantial influence over production and export channels. Beneficiation rules have increased state leverage but have not fully resolved ownership and transparency concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Power, Currency, and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, currency instability, and sanctions-related financial restrictions raise the cost of sovereign resource development. Zimbabwe remains dependent on external buyers, equipment, and payment routes.
